source_table: Appendix B narrative, section B.1 Absorption (text immediately following Table B-2; NOT carried in any numbered table)
route: oral (PFOA mixed into foods of differing nutritional composition, 7-day feeding)
matrix: liver (accumulation used as the bioavailability endpoint)
sd: 0.80 at the low end; 11.9 at the high end
model_or_method: in vivo comparison of liver PFOA accumulation after feeding PFOA in food mixtures (meat, seafood, milk, fruits/vegetables) versus in water
epa_notes: EPA: 'PFOA bioavailability relative to water ranged from 4.30 +/- 0.80 to 69.0 +/- 11.9% and was negatively correlated with lipid content (r = 0.76).' The authors suggest sorption by free fatty acids in foods could limit PFOA access to intestinal transporters, and that cations in the gastrointestinal tract such as Ca2+ and Mg2+ can complex PFOA promoting partitioning to the lipid phase. EPA's own conclusion: 'PFOA bioavailability is strongly influenced by diet, with high fat diets associated with reduced absorption, and that an important factor influencing PFOA bioaccessibility is colloidal stability in intestinal solutions.' This is the ONLY quantitative bioavailability figure anywhere in Appendix B - Table B-2 itself reports no bioavailability value, only Cmax and Tmax. A 16-fold range of relative bioavailability driven by diet is a large and under-recognised source of variability in oral PFOA dosimetry.
discrepancy_flag: NOT IN ANY NUMBERED EPA TABLE and not held in any db/ CSV checked - new to the project. The vehicle/matrix dependence (16-fold) is of the same order as the species and sex effects the project tracks, and applies to every oral animal dose in db/animal_halflife_measured.csv. Note the correlation is reported as r = 0.76 for a NEGATIVE correlation, i.e. the sign is stated in words but not in the coefficient.

source_table: Appendix B narrative, section B.1 Absorption (text immediately following Table B-2)
route: in vitro digestion of food matrices (0.3 g food, sample/solution ratio 1:97.5)
model_or_method: unified BARGE method (UBM) of Smith et al. (2012), applied to food instead of soil
epa_notes: EPA reports bioaccessibility varied by method: 8.7-73% for UBM, 9.8-99% for PBET, 21-114% for IVD. Bioaccessibility was negatively correlated with lipid content for the UBM method (r = 0.82) but NOT for the other methods (r = 0.11-0.22). EPA suggests UBM can be used to model bioaccessibility, possibly because it is associated with higher lipolysis and better mimics cations in gastrointestinal fluid, which may lower the potential to form stable micelles relative to PBET and IVD.
